items.title: 1. The app reads the account key
items.text:
The app asks the modern API for configuration:

GET /v1/private/{country}/{language}/{deviceId}/{appType}/{version}/{deviceType}/{aid}/common/getConfig?keys=PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG

The answer contains the RSA public key as base64 DER. The app uses it to encrypt fields such as encryptAccount, encryptPwd, encryptEmail, and the backup address before they leave the phone. The private key never leaves the server.

Bumper serves the public half at the same path. The key is generated once and stored in BUMPER_ACCOUNT_KEY (default ${BUMPER_DATA}/account.key) with mode 0600. It is separate from the TLS server key on purpose: the app needs RSA, the default TLS key is EC, and rotating the TLS certificate must not rotate the account key.

items.title: 2. The app logs in
items.text:
The modern login path is:

GET /v2/private/{country}/{language}/{deviceId}/{appType}/{version}/{deviceType}/{aid}/user/login2

The request carries encryptAccount and encryptPwd, plus the signing query parameters described below. Bumper decrypts the account name, resolves or creates one account, binds the app device id, and issues a portal token. The answer contains accessToken, uid (A), ucUid (U), loginName, username, country, and the response fields expected by the app.

If the account is new, the cloud may answer with loginResult: HIGH_RISK and loginRiskScene: NEW_DEVICE, and the app asks for an email code before it continues. Bumper answers success directly.

items.title: 3. The app exchanges the account token for an IoT token
items.text:
The app calls the OpenAPI host:

GET /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode?uid={uid}&accessToken={token}&bizType=ECOVACS_IOT&deviceId={deviceId}

The answer is an IT token:

{
    "code": "0000",
    "data": {
        "authCode": "GLOBAL_APP_ECOVACS_IOT_<32 hex>",
        "ecovacsUid": "<user id>"
    }
}

Despite the field name, this authCode is the IT token. It is attached to the token row identified by the presented access token. The app then posts it to the legacy login:

POST /newauth.do
{"todo": "OLoginByITToken", "itToken": "GLOBAL_APP_ECOVACS_IOT_<32 hex>"}

The answer is the real auth code:

{ "todo": "result", "result": "ok", "authCode": "<32 hex>" }

items.title: 4. The app gets OAuth tokens
items.text:
The auth code is exchanged on the legacy API:

GET /api/appsvr/oauth_callback?state={"cid":"<client id>"}&code={authCode}

The answer carries userId (I), access_token, refresh_token, and expire_at in milliseconds. The access token is a JWT. Its claims name the client (c = K), the user (u = I), the client resource (r = R), and the auth code (ac).

The app refreshes the pair through:

GET /api/appsvr/oauth/token?grant_type=refresh_token&refresh_token={jwt}&client_id={client id}

The refresh token is the same kind of JWT with t: "r"; the access token has t: "a".

items.title: 5. Later calls
items.text:
The modern API sends the access token as accessToken in the query string and also as authorization: Bearer <jwt> on some calls. The legacy API sends the opaque token as token or accessToken, depending on the endpoint.

The MQTT and XMPP transports resolve the presented IoT name and secret to the canonical account. With USE_AUTH=True, an access JWT must be signed by this Bumper instance. Connection rows retain their client/resource identity, so parallel app installations do not overwrite one another.

items.title: ✍️ Signing on the modern API
items.text:
The modern API adds five query parameters to every call:

Parameter Meaning authAppkey The app key. The app ships several, for the app and for OpenAPI. authTimespan The app clock in milliseconds, plus the server offset. authTimeZone The device timezone, for example GMT+2. requestId A per-request random id. authSign A digest over the app key, the sorted parameters, and a native secret.

The reference implementation builds the canonical string from the app key and the sorted query parameters, appends the secret, and digests the result. The keys and secrets are resolved from the native libeco-network.so library, not from Java constants.

Bumper ignores all five parameters. It does not reject a missing, stale, or wrong authSign. This is intentional for a LAN server: the app must work with a clock that is not synchronized to Ecovacs, and the signature protects a cloud account Bumper does not have.

The legacy API has a parallel scheme. com.ecovacs.lib_iot_client sends appid, ts, and sign, where sign is SHA1(appid + APP_SECRET + ts). Bumper does not verify those either. The app ships several app ids and secrets for the ecovacs and yeedi brands; Bumper does not need them.

items.title: Login and tokens
items.text:
bumper/web/auth_service.py:login serves both user/login and user/checkLogin on v1 and v2. The behavior is:

  1. Decrypt encryptAccount when present, then resolve the login name.
  2. Create an account with A, U, and I when the login name is new.
  3. Bind the app device id to that account.
  4. Remove expired token rows for the account.
  5. Generate a fresh opaque portal token and store a row for this login.
  6. Return uid=A and ucUid=U in the login document.

checkLogin never creates a user. An unknown name is resolved by the app device, and a request that matches neither is rejected. A check with a valid accessToken returns the same token. A check without a token issues a new one for the known account; an invalid supplied token is rejected. The portal token is opaque; it is not a JWT.

The portal-token lifetime is TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 days). Expiry removes the token row, including its IT token and auth code. A check with an expired portal token fails rather than silently replacing it. The modern /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode path requires a live portal token.

items.title: GetAuthCode
items.text:
There are two paths:

  • /v1/global/auth/getAuthCode and the private getAuthCode endpoint return the IT token in authCode. A live access token is required, and the IT token is attached to the token row that access token identifies.
  • api/users/user.do with todo: GetAuthCode returns the legacy auth code in code. It uses the token row named by the request when possible, or creates a portal-token row when no row is available.

Both paths resolve the presented account names to one user. A JWT claim is used to link accounts only after verify_jwt checks the signature, expiry, and access-token type. The IT token and auth code remain attached to the same client token row, so the next exchanges preserve the client boundary.

items.title: newauth.do
items.text:
bumper/web/single_paths.py:handle_new_auth accepts only todo: OLoginByITToken. It calls get_new_auth, which looks up the IT token, rejects an expired row, and returns the existing or newly generated auth code. The request's clientID and resource are stored on that same token and client row. The response is bound to the AUTH shape, so the answer is {"todo": "result", "result": "ok", "authCode": "..."}.

loginByItToken on api/users/user.do answers with userId=I, the portal token from the matching client row, and last, its remaining lifetime in milliseconds. The IT token is only the input of the exchange.

items.title: OAuth and JWT
items.text:
oauth_callback resolves the auth code to its token row, reads that row's client id and resource, and generates two JWTs with generate_jwt_helper:

  • access token: t: "a", expiry ACCESS_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 minutes)
  • refresh token: t: "r", expiry REFRESH_TOKEN_VALIDITY_SECONDS (30 days)

The token row remains until the refresh token expires. A successful OAuth exchange moves its expiry to the refresh token's expiry, and each successful refresh extends the session. This lets the app resume after an idle period without keeping the access JWT long-lived. Logout removes the row and revokes the refresh session.

The tokens are signed with the TLS server key (bumper_isc.server_key) and the algorithm in TOKEN_JWT_ALG. The default follows the certificate key type: ES256 for EC and RS256 for RSA.

bumper/web/jwt.py has two readers. get_jwt_details and extract_jwt_details decode the claims without checking the signature for the request context. verify_jwt loads the public key from the TLS certificate, checks the signature, the expiry, and the token type, and is the only reader that may be used as proof. The legacy GetAuthCode call, the refresh grant, and transport authentication use verify_jwt; a refresh token is not accepted where an access token is required. Account resolution also uses a JWT only after this check, even when USE_AUTH is off, because the claim can move a name between accounts.

items.title: The account key
items.text:
bumper/utils/account_key.py owns the RSA key used for encrypted account fields:

  • account_public_key() returns base64 DER, which is what PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG serves.
  • decrypt_account_field() decodes base64, decrypts with PKCS#1 v1.5, and returns the stripped UTF-8 text, or None on a malformed or foreign value.
  • _load_or_create() generates a 2048-bit RSA key on first use, writes it with O_EXCL at mode 0600, and re-reads it if another process won the race.

The private key is not used to sign JWTs or TLS certificates. It only decrypts the fields the app encrypts with the public key.

If the key changes, the app keeps the old public key for the life of its process. Force-stop the app after replacing account.key; otherwise the next email or password change returns 1008 because the ciphertext cannot be decrypted.

items.title: Email, password, and OTP
items.text:
Endpoint Behavior user/sendEmailVerifyCode Returns a fresh verifyId UUID. No mail is sent. user/checkEmailVerifyByScene Accepts EMAIL_VERIFY_CODE (default 666666). user/bindEmail2 Checks verifyCode, decrypts encryptEmail, stores it as email. user/addBackupEmail Decrypts encryptEmail and stores it as backup_email. user/modifyPassword Returns success with data: null. The password is not stored. device/otp/generate Returns a six digit code and stores it for DEVICE_OTP_TTL_SECONDS. device/verify/check Accepts the code while it is in the TTL.

bindEmail2 and addBackupEmail use claimed_userid, which reads userid, uid, a userid header, or the auth query object. None of those is signed. The address is stored only, not verified against a mailbox.

The OTP flow is equally local: the code is generated, returned to the caller, and accepted for the TTL. It is not a security control against a LAN peer.

items.title: Robot transports
items.text:
The app reaches the robot through XMPP or MQTT, depending on the model.

XMPP (bumper/xmpp/xmpp.py)

  • The app and the robot connect over TLS on port 5223.
  • SASL PLAIN carries an authzid, the user id, and a password. The password is either a bare secret or 0/<resource>/<secret>. Bumper reads the user id and the resource from the NUL-separated payload and joins the rest of the password after the resource, because a JWT never contains /.
  • A client with a devclass is a robot: Bumper stores it as a bot and accepts it without a token check.
  • A client without a devclass is the app. Bumper resolves the name through the portal token, the auth code, the IT token, or a signed access JWT to the canonical account and records the client under that account and resource. With USE_AUTH=True the secret must verify with identity.verify_transport_secret; with USE_AUTH=False the client is accepted and a name is adopted only when it already resolves or a valid secret links it.
  • The bound JID is <uid>@<devclass>.ecorobot.net/atom for a robot and <uid>@<server>/<resource> for the app.

MQTT (bumper/mqtt/server.py)

  • The broker listens on 1883 (plain) and 8883 (TLS).
  • A client id has the form <did>@<class id>/<resource>.
  • The class id decides the side: USER_CLASS_IDS (ecouser, bumper, USER) means app, anything else means robot.
  • The username may carry base64 app headers after a backtick; Bumper decodes them for logging and keeps the first segment as the username.
  • The helper bot uses a fixed client id and is accepted before any other check.
  • Bumper resolves the presented client name to the canonical account before it stores the client. Each client id/resource has its own row, so one account can keep parallel app installations and transport connections.
  • With USE_AUTH=False, Bumper accepts the password as-is. With USE_AUTH=True, the password must be a portal token, an auth code, an IT token, or a signed access JWT issued for that account.
  • A password file can also hold username:hash entries for broker users. It is read from ${BUMPER_DATA}/passwd.

The helper bot is Bumper's own client. It connects to the broker with the fixed HELPER_BOT_CLIENT_ID, bypasses authentication, and is the only component that writes the firmware version it learns from a robot into the database.

items.title: 📱 The app on the wire
items.text:
These facts come from the app package and are useful when a login fails:

  • The legacy client is com.ecovacs.lib_iot_client; it builds appid, ts, and sign in NetRequestUtil.
  • The modern client is com.eco.econetwork; SigningInterceptor and OpenSigningInterceptor add authAppkey, authTimespan, authTimeZone, requestId, and authSign.
  • The app reads PUBLIC.KEY.CONFIG before it encrypts account fields.
  • The app pins no certificate except the MQTT broker. The MQTT pin is embedded in a classes*.dex; scripts/app/apk-patch/patch-mqtt-trust.py removes it so Paho falls back to the platform store.
  • The NGIoT channel uses a native mbedTLS stack. It reads the system CA store and ignores the user store, so a user-installed Bumper CA does not cover it. If only that channel fails, suspect this before the certificate names.
  • The app's account screens need React Native and Hermes. A white screen there is usually a missing libhermes.so for the emulator ABI, not a Bumper auth failure.

The app package is the source for these details.

items.title: 🤖 The robot on the wire
items.text:
The robot does not log in with an Ecovacs account. It is provisioned with the server address and a local identity, and then it connects:

  • Older robots use XMPP with the serial number as the user id and atom as the resource.
  • Newer robots use MQTT with the serial number or device id as the client id, the model as the class id, and a resource name.
  • The auth code is the link from the account login to the transport. The robot receives it through the app's provisioning step, not through the cloud login.
  • TLS is verified against the CA the robot trusts. That CA is the one Bumper serves at /ca-certificates.tar.gz.

When Bumper sees a robot for the first time, the MQTT or XMPP login creates the bot record. Later calls use that record to resolve the serial number, model, and resource.

items.title: 🗺️ Code map

items.title: ⚠️ Known gaps
items.text:
• authSign is not verified. A wrong signature is accepted.
  • appid, ts, and the legacy sign are not verified.
  • The account password is ignored. Any password logs in.
  • Some request-context helpers decode JWT claims without checking the signature. Account linking and transport authentication use verify_jwt, which checks the signature, expiry, and token type.
  • USE_AUTH is a code constant, not an environment setting.
  • The auth code and IT token are removed when their portal/refresh session row expires. The legacy GetAuthCode path can create a fresh row; modern getAuthCode requires a live portal token and the client must log in again.
  • A logout with a recognized token revokes that token row and removes the client row it names. A logout with no token revokes every token and client for the account; an unknown supplied token does not log out unrelated clients, because the request is ignored.
  • The email verification code is fixed. Bumper never sends mail.
  • The OTP is returned to the caller and accepted for its TTL. It is a UX emulation, not a second factor.

These are deliberate for a self-hosted LAN replacement. Treat the network and the CA as the security boundary, not the application tokens.

items.title: Defeating Certificate Pinning in the Ecovacs Home App
items.text:
This guide covers how to make the Ecovacs Home Android app trust your own Bumper instance, so the app talks only to your LAN.

Disclaimer

Modifying the Ecovacs app may break future updates. Proceed at your own risk.

items.title: 📋 Methods
items.text:
Five ways to do this are documented below. Each needs different tools, so check its own Needs: line. Only the first is maintained.

Method Needs MQTT works Maintained Automated script docker yes yes Automated script (legacy) docker - no Manual apk-mitm node, npm, java, adb - no Manual apktool java, adb - no Manual android-unpinner python, java, adb - no

The three manual methods are reference material: they work in principle but are untested against current app versions. None of them applies the MQTT patch, so with those the web API works and MQTT robot control does not.

items.title: 🚀 Automated script (latest)
items.text: Needs: docker, and nothing else. The download, the patching and the signing all run inside a container, so your host stays clean. You also need adb and certs/ca.crt (see Create Certificates) for the device steps below, plus an arm64 device - see Device requirement.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
1. Downloads the app (XAPK or APK) and unpacks its splits.
  2. Sets android:debuggable="true" in the manifest, which activates the app's own <debug-overrides><certificates src="user"/>. That is what makes the platform trust your user-installed CA.
  3. Makes the certificate Ecovacs hardcodes for MQTT unusable, so that channel also falls back to the platform trust store.
  4. Runs zipalign and re-signs every split with a key kept in certs/.
  5. Verifies the result and prints the adb command to install it.

Steps 2 and 3 are both required. Without step 3 no command reaches an MQTT robot, because those commands are relayed over MQTT.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app.sh writes the installable APKs to data/<app-name>/.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app.sh

All of it runs in a container (bumper-apk-tool: JDK, Android build-tools, python3, curl). The only things written outside the container are data/<app-name>/ and the signing key certs/bumper-apk.jks; the download, the unpacked splits and the intermediate copies all disappear with the container. Editing a patcher only rebuilds the image's last layer.

1. Install the APKs. The script prints the exact command:

adb install-multiple --no-incremental data/<app-name>/*.apk

2. Install Bumper's CA on the phone as a user CA certificate: Settings → Security → Encryption & credentials → Install a certificate → CA certificate, and select certs/ca.crt. The script does not do this for you.

3. Point the app at your Bumper instance (see DNS Setup).

items.title: Device requirement
items.text:
An arm64 Android device, or an arm64 emulator. The account screens are React Native, so they need libhermes.so. base.apk contains no native code at all - every .so lives in the per-ABI split - and SoLoader searches only lib/<SUPPORTED_ABIS[0]> inside the APKs, one ABI, not a loop.

An x86_64 emulator reports SUPPORTED_ABIS: x86_64, arm64-v8a, and the app publishes no x86_64 build at any version, so libhermes.so is never found and the main activity dies in onCreate with SoLoaderDSONotFoundError. That is the white screen. Downgrading the app does not help: React Native and Hermes are already present in 3.11.0.

On an x86_64 host, an arm64-v8a system image can be booted under the emulator's bundled QEMU, which makes SUPPORTED_ABIS[0] arm64-v8a and the app install the arm64 split. Expect a slow boot (tens of minutes) - it is not an officially supported host architecture for that image.

items.title: The two patches
items.text:
1. android:debuggable="true" - the app ships a network_security_config.xml containing

<debug-overrides>
    <trust-anchors><certificates src="user"/></trust-anchors>
</debug-overrides>

Android applies <debug-overrides> to every domain, but only to a debuggable app. Setting that one flag is what makes the platform trust your user-installed CA, covering the web API, CodePush and the H5 pages. Nothing on those paths pins a certificate.

2. Neutralising the MQTT certificate pin - MQTT is the exception, and it is a real pin. The app's Paho fork builds its SSLSocketFactory from a certificate embedded in a classes*.dex, loads it into an empty KeyStore, and passes that to TrustManagerFactory.init(). A non-null, app-supplied KeyStore replaces the platform trust store entirely, so <debug-overrides> and every user CA are ignored and the handshake fails with CertPathValidatorException: Trust anchor for certification path not found.

The patch keeps a prefix of that embedded string - enough for the dex's string_ids table to stay sorted, which ART verifies on every launch - and fills the rest with a marker. CertificateFactory then rejects the result, the app's factory catches the exception and returns null, and Paho builds its SSLContext with null trust managers: the platform trust store again. The result contains no reference to Bumper's CA, so it stays valid when Bumper regenerates its certificates.

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• Re-signing changes the app's signature. The first install replaces any existing copy and clears its data, so you will have to log in again. Keep certs/bumper-apk.jks - the script reuses it on later runs so upgrades keep your session.
  • Set APK_URL near the top of the script to patch a different app version.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
"Trust anchor for certification path not found" in logcat, robot never reacts. The MQTT pin is still in place - the app was built with SKIP_MQTT_CA=1, or with an older version of the script. Rebuild and reinstall.

The app installs but the login screen is white. The main activity crashed. Check logcat for SoLoaderDSONotFoundError; that means the device ABI does not match the split, so use an arm64 device. The script prints the ABIs it produced at the end of the build.

docker run --rm --entrypoint python3 -v "$PWD/scripts/app/apk-patch:/p:ro" \
  bumper-apk-tool /p/test-patch-mqtt-trust.py

items.title: 🔧 Alternatives
items.text:
Warning

These predate the script above, do not apply the MQTT patch, and are not tested against current app versions. Prefer the script above.

items.title: 🚀 Automated script (legacy)
items.text:
Needs: docker only, like the script above.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app-legacy.sh runs apk-mitm in a container, which rewrites the APK so it trusts the CA you pass to it. Two differences from the latest script:

  • It embeds Bumper's CA into the app instead of relying on a user-installed one, so no certificate has to be installed on the phone - but it has to be rebuilt whenever Bumper regenerates its certificates.
  • It does not touch MQTT, so robot control will not work.

Kept because it patches differently, and is worth having when the latest script's manifest edit stops working on a future app version.

scripts/app/create-unpinned-app-legacy.sh

items.title: 🛠️ Manual apk-mitm Method
items.text:
Needs: node, npm, a JDK, adb, and certs/ca.crt.

This method leverages apk-mitm to patch the XAPK directly.

1. Download original XAPK:

curl -SLo ./data/eco.xapk \
  'https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?version=latest'

2. Patch with apk-mitm:

apk-mitm './data/eco.xapk' --certificate './certs/ca.crt'

3. Extract and install:

unzip -o './data/eco-patched.xapk' -d ./data/apks
adb install-multiple ./data/apks/*.apk

items.title: 🛠️ Manual apktool Method
items.text:
Needs: a JDK (for keytool, apksigner, java), apktool, curl, unzip, adb.

Full manual unpack, patch, and re-sign process.

1. Download and unpack:

cd ./data
APK_URL='https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?versionCode=127&nc=arm64-v8a'
APK_NAME="$(curl -sI -L "$APK_URL" | grep -o -E 'filename="[^"]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2)"
curl -SLo "$APK_NAME" "$APK_URL"
unzip "$APK_NAME" -d bump && cd bump

2. Prepare:

curl -SLo apktool.jar https://bitbucket.org/iBotPeaches/apktool/downloads/apktool_2.12.1.jar
export _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Djava.io.tmpdir=$HOME/.tmp"

3. Decode with apktool:

java -jar apktool.jar d 'com.eco.global.app.apk' --frame-path ~/.tmp/apktool-framework

4. Insert network security config:

Note

This step allows the app to trust user-installed certificates (e.g., your CA cert).

tee 'com.eco.global.app/res/xml/network_security_config.xml' > /dev/null <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system"/>
            <certificates src="user"/>
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>
</network-security-config>
EOF

5. Rebuild the APK:

sed -i 's/android:gravity="0x0"/android:gravity="center"/g' com.eco.global.app/res/layout/aa30_activity_air_auto.xml
java -jar apktool.jar b 'com.eco.global.app' --frame-path ~/.tmp/apktool-framework
cp 'com.eco.global.app/dist/com.eco.global.app.apk' 'com.eco.global.app.apk'

6. Sign the APK(s):

keytool -genkey -v -keystore bumper-key.jks -alias bumper-key \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000 \
  -storepass 123456 -keypass 123456 \
  -dname "CN=Bumper, OU=Bumper, O=Bumper, L=Home, S=Home, C=EU"

for apk in *.apk; do
  echo "Zipalign $apk"
  cp "$apk" "$apk.tmp"
  zipalign -p -f -v 4 "$apk.tmp" "$apk" 1>/dev/null
  rm -f "$apk.tmp"
done

for apk in *.apk; do
  echo "Signing $apk"
  apksigner sign \
    --ks bumper-key.jks \
    --ks-key-alias bumper-key \
    --ks-pass pass:123456 \
    --key-pass pass:123456 \
    --v1-signing-enabled true \
    --v2-signing-enabled true \
    --v3-signing-enabled true \
    "$apk"
done

7. Install on device:

adb install-multiple *.apk

items.title: 🛠️ Manual android-unpinner Method
items.text:
Needs: python3, pip/uv, a JDK, curl, unzip, adb.

Full manual unpack, patch, and re-sign process.

1. Download and unpack:

cd ./data
APK_URL='https://d.apkpure.net/b/XAPK/com.eco.global.app?versionCode=127&nc=arm64-v8a'
APK_NAME="$(curl -sI -L "$APK_URL" | grep -o -E 'filename="[^"]+"' | cut -d'"' -f2)"
curl -SLo "$APK_NAME" "$APK_URL"
unzip "$APK_NAME" -d bump && cd bump

2. Prepare:

# sudo apt install openjdk-21-jre-headless
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install uv
uv tool install git+https://github.com/mitmproxy/android-unpinner
export _JAVA_OPTIONS="-Djava.io.tmpdir=$HOME/.tmp"

3. Patch APKs:

android-unpinner patch-apks *.apk
for file in *.unpinned.apk; do mv -f "$file" "${file%.unpinned.apk}.apk"; done

4. Install on device:

adb install-multiple *.apk

items.title: Certificate Unpinning on Ecovacs Bot
items.text:
Disclaimer

Accessing and modifying your Ecovacs bot is risky and may permanently damage your device. These steps may void your warranty or violate your terms of service, and Ecovacs may refuse support for modified devices. Proceed entirely at your own risk!

Note

These instructions were tested only on a T10 PLUS. Details may differ on other models.

This guide explains two approaches to enable your Ecovacs bot to trust a self-signed certificate for use with a self-hosted Bumper server:

  • Option 1 (recommended, safer): replace certificate files on the bot - no firmware modification required.
  • Option 2 (advanced, unfinished): extract, modify, and reflash the root filesystem for deeper changes.

items.title: 🟢 Option 1: Simple Certificate Replacement
items.text: This method only updates certificate files on the device. No firmware unpacking or flashing is required.

items.title: 1. Start UART Console (on host)
items.text:
Connect to the bot's UART serial port.

Note

Adjust parameters as needed:

  • /dev/ttyACM0: device name may differ
  • --log / --log-file: optional, remove if you do not want logs

With picocom:

picocom /dev/ttyACM0 --flow n --baud 115200 --log ./b-capture-"$(date --iso-8601=seconds)".log

Or with tio:

tio /dev/ttyACM0 --flow none -b 115200 --log --log-file ./b-capture-"$(date --iso-8601=seconds)".log
T10 PLUS UART EXT-SOURCE UART

UART voltage

Never connect 5V to your UART adapter.

items.title: 2. Interrupt Boot and Enter Shell (on bot)
items.text:
On startup, interrupt into Hobot (press any key), then boot with updated bootargs:

setenv bootargs ${bootargs} init=/bin/bash
boot
Note

On some bots you need to hit a specific key mentioned during the boot-up process like: 

Hit key to stop autoboot('CTRL+C'):  0

Sometimes picocom does not work; in that case, try minicom. Keep pressing your key (e.g. CTRL+C) during the boot process until it is interrupted. 

minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 115200

items.title: 3. Initialize System Resources (on bot)
items.text:
Mount volumes and start required services:

export TERM=xterm-256color
mount -a

/etc/rc.d/pre_boot.sh start
/etc/rc.d/mount_data.sh start
/etc/rc.d/post_boot.sh start
/etc/rc.d/load_ko.sh start
/etc/rc.d/time_sync.sh start
Note

On some models the commands above fail. In that case, you can try to manually mount data by finding the correct partition in the boot logs. During boot, the partition table is logged on the console and looks similar to: 

GPT part:  0, name:            uboot, start:0x4000, size:0x2000
GPT part:  1, name:            trust, start:0x6000, size:0x2000
GPT part:  2, name:              eco, start:0x8000, size:0x3000
GPT part:  3, name:          reserve, start:0xb000, size:0x800
GPT part:  4, name:              sys, start:0xb800, size:0x1000
GPT part:  5, name:            boot1, start:0xc800, size:0x3000
GPT part:  6, name:          rootfs1, start:0xf800, size:0x40000
GPT part:  7, name:            boot2, start:0x4f800, size:0x3000
GPT part:  8, name:          rootfs2, start:0x52800, size:0x40000
GPT part:  9, name:             data, start:0x92800, size:0x5b7df

Identify the data partition (in the above example, index 9), add 1 to the index, and check for the device with ls /dev/rkflash0pX (replace X with your index; in the example below, /dev/rkflash0p10).

If the device exists, confirm it is the data filesystem before continuing. fsck.ext4 -y automatically approves filesystem repairs. If you proceed, you can mount it with:

mkdir -p /data
fsck.ext4 -y /dev/rkflash0p10
mount -t ext4 -o rw /dev/rkflash0p10 /data

items.title: 4. Replace Certificates (on bot)
items.text:
Note

Certificate changes made in this step may be reverted by a factory reset or firmware update. It is recommended to first connect your bot to the official Ecovacs cloud and complete the initial setup before replacing the certificates. If you ever reset or update the bot, you will need to repeat these certificate replacement steps.

After running the above scripts, /data is mounted. You can update the certificate files manually, or use the helper script from the host.

items.title: Option A: Helper script (recommended)
items.text:
The script writes the files over the existing UART shell session, so complete steps 1-3 first and make sure /data is mounted. Close picocom/tio/minicom before running it (only one program can hold the serial port), then reopen your terminal if you want to verify output on the bot.

On the host:

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install pyserial

python3 scripts/device/install-bot-certs-serial.py \
  --port /dev/ttyACM0 \
  --baud 115200 \
  --ca ./certs/ca.crt \
  --bumper ./certs/bumper.crt

The script overwrites /data/ca.crt and /data/ca-certificates/ca.pem with ca.crt, and appends a marked Bumper block (bumper.crt, then ca.crt) to /data/ca-certificates/ca-certificates.crt. Re-running replaces its previous marked block to avoid duplicates. Verify the BUMPER_WROTE/BUMPER_APPENDED/BUMPER_DONE markers on the bot, then reboot.

items.title: Option B: Manual update
items.text:
On your host, open the following files in a text editor:

  • ./certs/ca.crt
  • ./certs/bumper.crt

On the bot (UART shell), use an editor like vi or cat > to paste the contents into the correct files:

  • Overwrite /data/ca.crt with the contents of ./certs/ca.crt
  • Overwrite /data/ca-certificates/ca.pem with the contents of ./certs/ca.crt
  • For /data/ca-certificates/ca-certificates.crt, append the contents of ./certs/bumper.crt and then ./certs/ca.crt to the end of the file (do not remove existing entries; just add these two certs at the end, in this order)

Tip

You can use vi /data/ca-certificates/ca-certificates.crt and paste at the end, or append with cat >> /data/ca-certificates/ca-certificates.crt. Make sure to save and exit after pasting.

Your bot should now trust your self-signed certificates. Reboot and test connectivity to your Bumper server.

items.title: 🟡 Option 2: Full Root Filesystem Modification (Advanced)
items.text:
Not ready

This section is incomplete and not fully tested. Proceed only if you know what you are doing. More research/reverse engineering is required, especially for step 4. Flash Modified Rootfs Back to Bot -> b. Download and Flash on Bot.

If the simple method does not work, you may need to modify the root filesystem. This is riskier and can brick your device if done incorrectly.

items.title: 1. (Optional) Setup WiFi (on bot)
items.text: If you need network access on the bot, set up WiFi:

items.title: a. Load WiFi Firmware
items.text: /etc/rc.d/wifi.sh start

items.title: b. Connect to WiFi
items.text:
Note

Replace placeholders with your actual values:

  • <YOUR_SSID>
  • <YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD>
  • <YOUR_BOT_IP> (e.g., 192.168.112.57)
  • <YOUR_GATEWAY_IP> (e.g., 192.168.112.1)
mkdir -p /tmp/wpa_ctrl
echo "ctrl_interface=/tmp/wpa_ctrl" > /tmp/wpa_supplicant.conf

wpa_passphrase '<YOUR_SSID>' '<YOUR_WIFI_PASSWORD>' >> /tmp/wpa_supplicant.conf

wpa_supplicant -B -i wlan0 -c /tmp/wpa_supplicant.conf -f /tmp/wpa.log -s
ifconfig wlan0 '<YOUR_BOT_IP>' netmask 255.255.255.0 up
route add default gw '<YOUR_GATEWAY_IP>'

items.title: a. Dump Root Filesystem
items.text: dd if=/dev/ubi0_0 of=/tmp/rootfs.img bs=1M

items.title: b. (Optional) Backup Other Partitions
items.text:
dd if=/dev/ubi1_0 of=/tmp/data.img bs=1M
dd if=/dev/ubi2_0 of=/tmp/sysinfo.img bs=1M
dd if=/dev/ubi3_0 of=/tmp/ai_model.img bs=1M
tar -czf /tmp/data.tar.gz -C /data .

items.title: c. Serve Files for Download
items.text: cd / && httpd -p 8080

items.title: 3. Download and Extract Root Filesystem Dump (on host)
a. Download Root Filesystem to Host
items.text:
Note

Replace <YOUR_BOT_IP> with your bot's actual IP address.

curl -Lo rootfs.img http://<YOUR_BOT_IP>:8080/tmp/rootfs.img

items.title: b. (Optional) Download Other Partitions to Host
items.text:
curl -Lo data.img http://<YOUR_BOT_IP>:8080/tmp/data.img
curl -Lo sysinfo.img http://<YOUR_BOT_IP>:8080/tmp/sysinfo.img
curl -Lo ai_model.img http://<YOUR_BOT_IP>:8080/tmp/ai_model.img
curl -Lo data.tar.gz http://<YOUR_BOT_IP>:8080/tmp/data.tar.gz

You can extract or inspect these optional backup partitions with tools like ubireader_extract_files, strings, or unsquashfs:

ubireader_extract_files data.img
cat sysinfo.img | strings
unsquashfs -d ai_model ./ai_model.img
mkdir -p data && tar -xzf ./data.tar.gz -C data

items.title: c. Extract and Modify Rootfs
items.text:
unsquashfs -d rootfs ./rootfs.img
# ... edit rootfs as needed ...
mksquashfs rootfs rootfs_mod.img -noappend -root-owned -p '/dev d 755 0 0' -p '/dev/console c 600 0 0 5 1'

a. Start HTTP Server on Host
items.text: python3 -m http.server 8080

ubi_atomic_update_leb /dev/ubi2_0 -i "boot_mode2" -n 0

items.text:
Disclaimer

Accessing and modifying your Ecovacs Goat is risky and may permanently damage your device. These steps may void your warranty or violate your terms of service, and Ecovacs may refuse support for modified devices. Proceed entirely at your own risk!

Note

These instructions were tested only on a Goat O500. Details may differ on other models.

items.title: 🟢 Simple Certificate Replacement
items.text: This method only updates certificate files on the device. No firmware unpacking or flashing is required.

items.title: 1. Start UART Console (on host)
items.text:
Connect to the Goat UART serial port.

Note

Adjust parameters as needed:

  • /dev/ttyACM0: device name may differ
  • --log / --log-file: optional, remove if you do not want logs

With picocom:

picocom /dev/ttyACM0 --flow n --baud 115200 --log ./b-capture-"$(date --iso-8601=seconds)".log

Or with tio:

tio /dev/ttyACM0 --flow none -b 115200 --log --log-file ./b-capture-"$(date --iso-8601=seconds)".log
Goat O500 UART

Pinout (O500):

1/6 2/7 3/8 4/9 5/10 5V (RED) NC NC NC GND UART TX UART RX NC NC NC

UART voltage

Never connect the 5 V pin to your UART adapter.

items.title: 2. Interrupt Boot and Enter Hobot (on Goat)
items.text:
During power-up, interrupt the boot process to enter Hobot (press any key).

Note

On some Goat you need to hit a specific key mentioned during the boot-up process like: 

Hit key to stop autoboot('CTRL+C'):  0

Sometimes picocom does not work; in that case, try minicom. Keep pressing your key (e.g. CTRL+C) during the boot process until it is interrupted. 

minicom -D /dev/ttyUSB0 -b 115200

items.title: 3. Locate the eMMC and userdata Partition
items.text:
Unlike older Ecovacs bots, Goat devices do not allow modifying bootargs to drop into Linux.

All changes are performed from U-Boot by directly accessing the eMMC.

items.title: 3.1 Select eMMC Device
items.text:
Device 0 is typically the internal eMMC.

# List all MMC devices
mmc list

# Select the device marked as eMMC (usually device 0)
mmc dev 0

Check write-protection status:

# Display eMMC details and write protection status
mmc info

Expected output:

Boot area 0 is not write protected

items.title: 3.2 Identify userdata Partition
items.text:
List partitions:

mmc part

On Goat O500, userdata is typically:

  • Partition 16 (hex 0x10 → mmc 0:10)

Verify filesystem access:

# List root directory of userdata partition
ext4ls mmc 0:10 /

You should see directories such as /certs.

items.title: 3.3 Verify Existing Certificate Location
items.text:
Before writing anything, confirm that the existing certificate file exists and is readable.

Note

If UART logging is enabled, the original certificate contents will also be captured in the UART log, which effectively serves as a backup.

# Load existing certificate into RAM
ext4load mmc 0:10 0xc2600000 /certs/master.pem

# Dump loaded content to verify correctness
md.b 0xc2600000 <FILE-SIZE-HEX>

# Optional: inspect full CA bundle
# ext4load mmc 0:10 0xc2600000 /certs/ca-certificates.crt

items.title: 4. Replace Certificates (on Goat)
items.text:
The replacement is done by:

  1. Injecting the new certificate into RAM via UART
  2. Writing it back into the userdata partition

items.title: 4.1 Inject Certificate into RAM (on host)
items.text:
Close picocom/tio/minicom before running the script (only one program can hold the serial port). The script sends U-Boot mw.l/mw.b commands to inject the PEM into RAM, then prints the ext4write command. It does not run ext4write itself (run that in the Goat U-Boot shell).

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install pyserial

python3 scripts/device/install-goat-certs-serial.py \
  --port /dev/ttyACM0 \
  --cert ./certs/ca.crt \
  --target /certs/master.pem \
  --mmc-part 10

Adjust --port, --cert, --target (e.g. /certs/ca-certificates.crt if you need to replace the bundle), and --mmc-part for your model (Goat O500 userdata is typically mmc 0:10). Use --dry-run to print the planned writes and the ext4write/md.b commands without opening the serial port.

items.title: 4.2 Write Certificate to eMMC (on Goat)
items.text:
Execute the printed command in U-Boot:

# Write injected certificate from RAM into userdata
ext4write mmc 0:10 0xC2600000 /certs/master.pem <FILE-SIZE-HEX>

Verify write success:

# Reload certificate from eMMC
ext4load mmc 0:10 0xc2600000 /certs/master.pem
# Compare with injected content
md.b 0xc2600000 <FILE-SIZE-HEX>

items.title: 5. Reboot
items.text:
reset

The Goat now trusts your custom CA.

items.text:
• Always backup your data before making changes.
  • Firmware updates or factory resets may overwrite certificates.
  • For certificate creation, see Create Certificates.
  • For more context, see Architecture and App Certificate Unpinning.

items.title: Android Sniffing on Ubuntu with mitmproxy
items.text: This guide walks you through setting up an Android emulator on Ubuntu, installing a custom CA certificate, and using mitmproxy to intercept traffic. It also includes an optional Python addon for enhanced output filtering.

items.title: 📋 Prerequisites
items.text:
• Ubuntu 22.04+
  • Docker (for running mitmproxy)
  • Android Studio (for emulator and ADB)
  • CA certificate (ca.crt and ca.pem) in the ./certs/ folder
    • Created by bash scripts/certs/create-cert.sh or by Bumper at startup; see Certificates

items.title: 🚀 Install Android Studio & SDK
items.text:
Install Android Studio via Snap:

sudo snap install android-studio --classic

Launch Android Studio and follow the initial setup to install the SDK and platform-tools.

Tip

Install the SDK under ~/.android/Sdk for consistency.

items.title: 🖥️ Create an Emulator
items.text:
1. Open AVD Manager (Virtual Device Manager).
  2. Click Create Virtual Device.
  3. Choose a device (e.g., Pixel 6 Pro) without Google Play Store.
  4. Select a system image with API 28 (Android 9 Pie) or lower to allow system CA installation.

items.title: 🔧 Prepare the Emulator
items.text:
(Optional) Disable Quickboot file-backed feature (can help with BTRFS-related emulator issues):

echo "QuickbootFileBacked = off" >> ~/.android/advancedFeatures.ini

List available AVDs:

~/.android/Sdk/emulator/emulator -list-avds

Start the emulator with root access and writable system. Replace <AVD_NAME> with an AVD from the list above:

~/.android/Sdk/emulator/emulator \
    -avd <AVD_NAME> \
    -writable-system \
    -no-boot-anim \
    -gpu host \
    -cores 4 \
    -memory 4096

Restart ADB as root and remount:

~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb root
~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb remount

items.title: 🔒 Install the CA Certificate
items.text:
Push your custom CA into the emulator's system trust store. The emulator must be started with -writable-system and ADB remounted as root (see Prepare the Emulator):

HASH=$(openssl x509 -inform PEM -subject_hash_old -in certs/ca.crt | head -1)
~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb push certs/ca.crt "/system/etc/security/cacerts/${HASH}.0"
~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb reboot
~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb wait-for-device

Note

On Android 10 and newer the system partition is read-only. Install the CA as a user certificate instead, and use an app that trusts user CAs (for example the patched app from Defeating Certificate Pinning).

items.title: 📱 Install the Target App and Proxy App
1️⃣ Install Ecovacs Home App
items.text:
Download and install version 2.4.1 of the Ecovacs Home APK:

Note

To reverse newer app versions, you need to unpin the certificate first. See Defeating Certificate Pinning for instructions.

  • Ecovacs Home on APKPure (older versions may be easier to inspect; newer versions may require certificate pinning bypass)

Install the app on the emulator:

~/.android/Sdk/platform-tools/adb install <path/to/Ecovacs_Home_2.4.1.apk>

Tip

Drag-and-drop the APK onto the emulator window.

items.title: 2️⃣ Install SOCKS5 Proxy App
items.text:
Install a SOCKS5 proxy client (e.g., Super Proxy):

  • Use a SOCKS5 proxy app on the emulator/device (for example, Proxy Server on APKPure or another SOCKS5 client; verify the app/package before installing).

items.title: 🌐 Configure Proxy on Android
items.text:
In the emulator's network or proxy app settings:

  • Protocol: SOCKS5
  • Host: <YOUR_SERVER_IP>
  • Port: 1080

This routes all emulator traffic through mitmproxy.

items.title: ⚙️ Run mitmproxy with Docker Compose / Swarm
items.text:
The repository includes docker-compose-mitm.yaml with pre-defined mitmproxy settings and helper scripts. It uses certs/ca.pem, so make sure your Bumper certificates exist.

Docker Compose

docker compose -f docker-compose-mitm.yaml up -d

Docker Swarm

Alias

This uses the docker-swarm-compose alias. Pass the compose file with -f; setting COMPOSE_FILE is not enough. The final argument is the stack name.

docker-swarm-compose -f docker-compose-mitm.yaml mitm

Access http://localhost:8081 to inspect traffic.

items.title: 🐍 Optional: Python Script Addons
items.text:
docker-compose-mitm.yaml mounts helper scripts from configs/ (mitm-cmd.py, mitm-mqtt.py, mitm-dns.py). Script loading is controlled by environment variables, so you can enable only what you need:

Variable Default Script Purpose MITM_SCRIPT_CMD 1 /tmp/mitm-cmd.py Capture/filter HTTP command traffic MITM_SCRIPT_MQTT 0 /tmp/mitm-mqtt.py MQTT sniffing MITM_SCRIPT_DNS 1 /tmp/mitm-dns.py DNS helper/filtering

Examples:

# Enable MQTT sniffing in addition to defaults
MITM_SCRIPT_MQTT=1 docker compose -f docker-compose-mitm.yaml up -d

# Only the MQTT script
MITM_SCRIPT_CMD=0 MITM_SCRIPT_MQTT=1 MITM_SCRIPT_DNS=0 docker compose -f docker-compose-mitm.yaml up -d

You can also set MITM_WEB_PW to change the mitmweb password (default: mitm) and MITM_PATH for capture output.

items.title: 🛠️ Troubleshooting
items.text:
• SSL errors: Verify the CA hash and placement.
  • Emulator won't root: Use API 28 or lower with -writable-system.
  • App 2003 errors: Launch the app once without proxy to fetch initial data.

items.text: When opening a discussion, include the classid, model, firmware version, transport, and whether the official app or only a client can control the robot. Logs with DEBUG_BUMPER_LEVEL=DEBUG are useful when available.

items.title: Troubleshooting notes
items.text:
The usual reasons, in the order they are worth checking:

  1. Certificate pinning. The robot ignores the CA and trusts only the certificate it shipped with. Check the per-device guides: bot, GOAT, app.
  2. Key type. Some robots only offer RSA in their client hello while Bumper generates an EC key. Set CERT_KEY_TYPE=rsa and CERT_RSA_KEY_SIZE=2048.
  3. Transport. Older models speak XMPP, newer ones MQTT, the newest ones NGIoT. A model on the wrong transport connects and then answers nothing.
  4. DNS. A robot that still reaches the Ecovacs cloud is not talking to Bumper. See DNS Setup.

items.title: 🐳 Deploy Bumper
items.text: Manage Bumper with Docker: pull the official image, deploy with Compose or Swarm, build custom images, or run directly.

items.title: 🔧 Prerequisites
items.text:
TLS certificates

The checked-in docker-compose.yaml and docker-compose-traefik.yaml load ca.crt, bumper.crt, and bumper.key from $PWD/certs/* as read-only Docker configs, so the files must exist before you deploy. Create them, then install certs/ca.crt on the clients:

bash scripts/certs/create-cert.sh
# add --rsa if your robot requires RSA keys

Key types, SANs, and certificate generation are covered in Certificates.

Environment variables:

Create a .env file with at least the following:

# 'overlay' for Docker Swarm, 'bridge' for plain Docker Compose
NETWORK_MODE=overlay

# required by the Compose file
BUMPER_ANNOUNCE_IP=192.168.0.100  # your server's local IP

Full environment variable reference: Environment Variables

items.title: ✨ Pull the Official Image
items.text:
docker pull ghcr.io/mvladislav/bumper:latest

See the package on GitHub Container Registry here.

items.title: 👤 Container User
items.text:
Bumper runs as the unprivileged user bumper (uid/gid 1000). In the checked-in Compose files, /bumper/data is the writable state volume and /bumper/certs is provided via read-only Docker configs.

A named volume takes ownership from the image and needs no manual step. The container starts as root, repairs ownership of writable mounted paths when it can (capabilities granted by the checked-in Compose files), and then drops to bumper. If you use a custom writable host directory, ensure it is readable or writable as needed by uid/gid 1000.

items.title: 🚀 Docker Swarm Deployment
items.text:
Step 1 - Clone the repository

git clone https://github.com/MVladislav/bumper.git
cd bumper

Step 2 - Initiate Docker in Swarm mode

docker swarm init

Step 3 - Start services

Alias

This uses the docker-swarm-compose alias, which is maintained in the dotfiles repository. Pass the compose file with -f; setting COMPOSE_FILE is not enough. The final argument is the stack name.

# pulls ghcr.io/mvladislav/bumper, tag from VERSION_BUMPER (default "latest")
docker-swarm-compose deebot

# with a non-default compose file (for example the Traefik variant)
docker-swarm-compose -f docker-compose-traefik.yaml deebot

# or plain Docker Compose: builds the image from this checkout
docker compose up -d

Step 4 - Access the UI

Visit https://ecovacs.net/ in your browser.

items.title: 🗂️ Extra data files (voices, CodePush)
items.text:
Voice files and CodePush packages are large and are not part of the image or repository, so they live in the data volume: /bumper/data/voices and /bumper/data/codepush inside the container (BUMPER_VOICES and BUMPER_CODEPUSH override the paths). Features explains what needs them.

The files either live in that volume already or are copied into it:

docker cp ./data/voices/.   <container>:/bumper/data/voices/
docker cp ./data/codepush/. <container>:/bumper/data/codepush/

With Swarm the named volume is local to a node, so the files have to exist on the node that runs the task (or be copied into the volume there).

The files are downloaded by the maintainer scripts; see Static Data Update.

items.title: 🛠 Build a Custom Image
items.text:
Step 1 - Clone the repository (if not already done)

git clone https://github.com/MVladislav/bumper.git
cd bumper

Step 2 - Build

# same name and tag the Compose file expects
docker build -t ghcr.io/mvladislav/bumper:latest .

Requires Docker ≥17.09 or Podman.

items.title: 🎯 Direct Docker Run
items.text:
Step 1 - Create a Docker volume

docker volume create bumper_data

(Or use a host directory: -v /path/to/data:/bumper/data.)

Step 2 - Run the container

docker run -it \
  --mount source=bumper_data,target=/bumper/data \
  -v $PWD/certs:/bumper/certs \
  -p 443:443 -p 8007:8007 -p 1883:1883 -p 8883:8883 -p 5223:5223 \
  --name bumper \
  ghcr.io/mvladislav/bumper:latest
  • Volumes: bumper_data holds Bumper state. Mount a writable host directory at /bumper/certs if you want generated certificates to persist across container recreation; you can also pre-create certificates with scripts/certs/create-cert.sh. Without a persistent writable certs mount, a new container may generate a new CA and clients that trusted the old CA will fail.
  • Ports: 443 (HTTPS), 8007 (HTTP), 1883 (plain MQTT), 8883 (MQTT over TLS), 5223 (XMPP over TLS)

For advanced Docker parameters (resource limits, secrets, configs), see the Environment Variables.

items.title: ✨ Features
items.text: Bumper reimplements selected Ecovacs cloud features locally. Availability depends on the robot model, firmware, app version, region, and whether required data files are present.

items.title: 🗣️ Voice Languages
items.text:
The official app can switch a robot's voice language. Bumper serves the voice metadata the app requests and the voice file the robot downloads.

What is needed

  • Voice metadata is part of Bumper's static data (voices.json).
  • The actual voice files are not stored in the repository. Fetch metadata/files with the maintainer script described in Static Data Update (update-eco-voices.sh).
  • Place the downloaded files where Bumper can read them. By default that is ${BUMPER_DATA}/voices (BUMPER_VOICES overrides the path). In Docker, put them in the data volume; see Docker.

Behavior

  • Bumper serves voice metadata/language information to the app and serves voice files from BUMPER_VOICES.
  • If a requested voice file is missing, Bumper logs a warning and returns 404 for that file. The robot keeps its current language instead of installing the new one.

  • At startup Bumper logs how many voice files it found, for example:

    INFO :: bumper.web.server - Voice files :: 13 in '/bumper/data/voices'

items.title: 🗺️ Work Logs and Clean Maps
items.text:
After a cleaning job, supported robots can upload job data and map data. Bumper stores that data and serves it back to the app and its own web UI.

In the official app

  • The work-log list is served by /app/dln/api/log/clean_result/list (for supported logType=clean requests).
  • When a stored map exists for a job, Bumper provides an image URL for that job.

In the Bumper web UI

  • Open Clean Logs and use a job's menu to choose Show map. The map is rendered and displayed over the page.

Storage and limits

  • Uploaded pictures and cleaned maps are stored per robot. When the per-device limit is reached, older items are removed on new uploads. Configure with PHOTO_MAX_PER_DEVICE.
  • Clean-log entries are stored per robot and pruned to CLEAN_LOG_MAX_PER_DEVICE.
  • Support depends on what the robot/app uploads and requests. Not every model or app flow exposes the same history.

items.title: 📱 App Updates (CodePush)
items.text:
The official app can load JavaScript bundles from CodePush instead of only using the bundles shipped in the APK. Bumper answers the app's update check from its static data (updateCheck.json and updateCheck_mapping.json).

Serving packages locally

  • By default the update check points the app at the cloud for the package download. Set CODEPUSH_LOCAL_PACKAGE=true to make Bumper answer with its own download URL: https://<codepush-base host>/api/appsvr/codepush/download/<deployment_key>. That host is covered by the wildcard DNS override.
  • The package files have to be in ${BUMPER_DATA}/codepush (BUMPER_CODEPUSH overrides the path) and are named after their deployment key. scripts/data/3-update-eco-codepush-packages.sh writes them there. See Docker: Extra data files for copying them into a container or Swarm node.
  • If a package is missing, the download answers 404 and the app keeps its current bundle.
  • The packages are large and are not part of the image or repository. Refresh them with the script above; see Static Data Update.

CodePush ships app logic

A CodePush bundle is executable app code, not just an image or a translation file. A stale or mismatched updateCheck.json entry can make the app behave incorrectly. Keep the metadata and the packages in sync with the app version you are running.

items.title: ⚙️ Related configuration
items.text: BUMPER_VOICES, BUMPER_CODEPUSH, CODEPUSH_LOCAL_PACKAGE, PHOTO_MAX_PER_DEVICE, and CLEAN_LOG_MAX_PER_DEVICE change this page's behavior; each is described in Environment Variables. The data files are refreshed with the scripts in Static Data Update.

items.title: 📲 Using Bumper with the Official Android/iOS App
items.text:
You can use the official "Ecovacs" or "Ecovacs Home" app to control your robot through your local Bumper server. This requires:

  • DNS overrides as described in DNS Setup.
  • Trusting Bumper's CA certificate on your device (generated via Certificates).

Note

Functionality may vary by app version, region, and robot model. Some features depend on cloud services and may not work with Bumper.

items.title: iOS (iOS 10+)
items.text:
1. Transfer certs/ca.crt (PEM format) to your device (for example, email or AirDrop).
  2. Tap the file to open the install prompt.
  3. In Settings → Profile Downloaded, tap Install and enter your passcode.
  4. Go to Settings → General → About → Certificate Trust Settings.
  5. Enable full trust for Bumper CA.

items.title: Android 6 and older (API 23 and below)
items.text:
For older releases, install the CA as a user certificate:

  1. Copy certs/ca.crt to device storage.
  2. Go to Settings → Security → Install from device storage.
  3. Select the certificate, name it, and choose VPN and apps.

items.title: Android 7 and newer (API 24 and above)
items.text:
Apps that target API 24 or newer do not trust user-installed CAs by default. There are two ways around that:

  • Use the patched app. Its android:debuggable="true" flag activates the app's own <debug-overrides>, which makes it trust a user CA. Install ca.crt as a user certificate, then follow Certificate Pinning Bypass (APP) for the app's MQTT pin.

  • On Android 9 and lower, install the CA into the system store with adb root. This needs a debuggable or rooted build; production firmware rejects adb root:

    # Start adb as root
adb root
# Remount /system writable
adb remount
# Push CA into system store
adb push certs/ca.crt "/system/etc/security/cacerts/$(openssl x509 -inform PEM -subject_hash_old -in certs/ca.crt | head -1).0"
adb reboot

    Verify in Settings → Security → Trusted credentials → System.

    From Android 10 (API 29) the system partition is read-only, so a system-store install is not an option there; use the patched app instead.

Tip

If your device or app still rejects the certificate, consider certificate-pinning bypass or a rooted-device approach.

Tip

For emulators, see the Prepare the Emulator section in Sniffing & Reverse Engineering.

Note

App-side pinning and native TLS stacks can still block specific paths even when SANs are correct. Check device logs when a single host fails. See DNS Setup.

items.title: ⚙️ Configure the App
items.text:
1. Launch Ecovacs / Ecovacs Home.
  2. On the login screen, enter any email/password (6+ characters).
  3. If your robot is connected to Bumper, it can appear in the device list.
  4. Tap the robot; the app communicates with it through the services Bumper provides.

Note

Bumper accepts logins for compatibility; real Ecovacs credentials are not validated by Bumper.

items.title: ✨ Features
items.text: Voice language changes and work logs/maps are documented in Features. These features depend on required data/files and supported robot/app behavior.

items.title: 🛠️ Troubleshooting
items.text:
• No robots found: confirm DNS overrides, reachability/proxy routing, and that Bumper is reachable. The web UI is a status view; robots appear only after they connect to Bumper. See Getting Started.
  • Login errors: ensure your CA is trusted and the HTTPS connection succeeds. Check app pinning/native TLS behavior when needed.
  • Missing features: some cloud-only functions are not implemented. Supported local features (for example, voice files or work logs/maps) may still require data files or model support. See Features.
